title: Ryan Colton is new AD at New Hampshire - USCHO.com
content: "Ryan has the vision, experience, and judgment to lead UNH athletics at a pivotal moment in college sports," said UNH president Elizabeth S. Chilton, via statement. "He understands the rapidly changing Division I landscape and what it will take to position our programs for sustained competitive success." Before joining Richmond, Colton began his collegiate athletics administrative career at Holy Cross, where he served as assistant athletics director. Previously, he was special assistant to the director of athletics at Providence. "The University of New Hampshire represents everything I value about higher education and intercollegiate athletics: a commitment to student success, access to opportunity and the pursuit of excellence," Colton said in a statement. The UNH men's hockey team is coming off a 14-20-1 season, where it went 8-15-1 in Hockey East. The UNH women's team was 16-16-3, 10-12-2 in Hockey East. Colton has also held several public service and legal positions, including serving as a city councilor and council president in Taunton, Mass., practicing law in private practice and serving as a staff member in the Massachusetts State Senate. Colton previously chaired the NCAA Division I Women's Golf Committee. He succeeds Allison Rich, who led UNH Athletics from 2022-26. Additional details regarding Colton's start date and introductory event will be announced at a later date, the school said.

Shares of health insurance companies, including Centene (CNC), slipped after-hours on Tuesday following a report that the Trump administration plans to end a federal subsidy program that has helped suppress Medicare Part D prescription drug plan premiums. The federal program is currently channeling an estimated $3.6 billion to insurers this year to keep Part D premiums in check. Officials told The Wall Street Journal that the support will expire after 2026 and will not be extended into 2027. Without the federal support, plan sponsors may pass increased costs to enrollees, potentially accelerating shifts toward Medicare Advantage plans that bundle drug benefits. An administration official quoted by the Journal projected that roughly one-quarter of Part D enrollees will see their premiums hold steady or decline in 2027, about 30% will face hikes under $10 a month, and the remaining 45% will largely see increases in the $11–$20 range. The subsidy primarily benefits insurers offering stand-alone Part D plans (PDPs). Companies with substantial PDP enrollment—UnitedHealth Group (UNH), CVS Health (CVS, via Aetna), Humana (HUM), Centene (CNC, via WellCare), and Molina Healthcare (MOH)—stand to lose this revenue stream. title: UnitedHealth UNH Stock Touches $430 as Improving Margins Boost Investor Confidence - FXLeaders
content: UnitedHealth Group’s fragile recovery is showing signs of losing momentum as investors remain wary of rising healthcare costs, regulatory uncertainty, and doubts over the sustainability of its improving margins. UnitedHealth Group’s recovery is beginning to look increasingly fragile as investors reassess whether the healthcare giant can sustain its recent improvement in earnings and margins. Although the stock rebounded sharply on Tuesday and climbed above $430, lingering concerns over medical costs, regulatory pressure, and the quality of the recent margin improvement continue to cloud the outlook. UnitedHealth shares staged a notable recovery from their March lows, eventually reclaiming the important $400 resistance level and moving above $430 on Tuesday. The rebound initially reflected renewed confidence that the worst of the company’s margin pressure may have passed. The optimism was reinforced by stronger-than-expected quarterly results. UnitedHealth reported revenue of $111.7 billion, up 2% year over year, while adjusted earnings per share reached $7.23, comfortably exceeding analyst expectations. The company also delivered an improvement in its Medical Care Ratio, which declined to 83.9% from 88.9% previously. UnitedHealthcare margins also expanded, suggesting that some of the intense cost pressures that previously weighed on profitability may be easing. However, the recovery story is far from convincing. One of the biggest concerns surrounding the rebound is whether UnitedHealth’s improved medical loss ratio reflects a sustainable operational recovery. Some of the improvement has been linked to the company deliberately exiting unprofitable markets rather than achieving broad-based efficiency gains. That distinction is important because a recovery driven partly by reducing exposure to loss-making businesses may not provide the same long-term growth potential. As a result, investors remain cautious about whether margins can continue improving once utilization pressures return. UnitedHealth received a boost after Morgan Stanley raised its price target to $468 from $453 while maintaining an overweight rating. The revision reflected expectations for improving utilization trends and more stable medical costs. Yet positive analyst sentiment has done little to eliminate broader concerns surrounding the stock. Berkshire Hathaway’s decision to exit its entire 3.3 million-share position earlier this year also remains a negative overhang, raising questions about earnings visibility and institutional confidence. The healthcare sector has also received some relief from stronger results at peers such as Centene, suggesting medical cost inflation could be moderating in parts of the industry. UnitedHealth gained additional support after the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services approved a 2.48% increase in Medicare Advantage payment rates for 2027. Given the company’s significant exposure to Medicare Advantage, the policy change could improve visibility around future revenue and profitability. Still, regulatory scrutiny remains elevated. Any renewed acceleration in medical utilization or healthcare costs could quickly undermine the recovery narrative. UnitedHealth Group shares have surged higher in the last two months, climbing back above the $400 level after beating Q1 earnings expectations and the Cantene news but failed to hold gains above that level. The move built on an earlier rebound in April, when the stock gained momentum following favorable policy developments. After a difficult period in early 2025, the recent price action has been bullish, sending UNH stock price above moving averages which have acted as support in 2026. The rally revived hopes of a broader recovery, especially after pushing above $400. The company has also taken steps to reinforce profitability, including reducing Medicare Advantage membership by approximately 1.3 million lives as part of an effort to improve efficiency and protect margins. While these actions support the stabilization narrative, they also highlight the ongoing trade-off between growth and profitability in a competitive and heavily regulated environment.

The University of New Hampshire has appointed Ryan Colton as its next director of athletics. Colton is a New England native who currently serves the University of Richmond as deputy athletic director and chief of staff. In total, the New England Law graduate has 15 years of experience as a senior leader in NCAA Division I athletics. He’s now charged with leading UNH’s 20-sport program in an era of shifting compliance regulations, name-image-likeness (NIL) compensation, a shrinking student body and decreases in state funding. “Ryan has the vision, experience and judgment to lead UNH athletics at a pivotal moment in college sports,” said UNH President Elizabeth S. Chilton in a press release. “He understands the rapidly changing Division I landscape and what it will take to position our programs for sustained competitive success. Just as important, he recognizes that athletics is an integral part of the university. His focus on strong connections across campus and on the whole student-athlete will help ensure our students succeed in competition, in the classroom, and in their lives after graduation.” Colton will be taking over for Allison Rich, who served as in the role from 2022 to 2026. Before joining UNH and Richmond, Colton was a special assistant to the athletic director at Providence College for two years while also serving as a city councilor in Taunton, Mass. He later became the assistant AD for compliance at Holy Cross for two years before joining Richmond in 2018. While at Richmond, he oversaw “business operations, human resources, legal affairs, compliance, NIL initiatives, student-athlete conduct and implementation of emerging NCAA policies,” according to the news release. title: The Architect’s Garden - University of New Hampshire
content: On a bright morning in May, Master Gardener Jan Litvin takes a brush to a concrete bird bath that had taken on a verdant hue. “I do like moss, but in its place,” says Litvin as her bristles scrape away the enterprising plant, which was seeking to overgrow the avian amenity in a backyard perennial garden at the Zimmerman House, one of two Frank Lloyd Wright-designed homes owned by the Currier Museum. Litvin is among 37 volunteers, who have all been through Extension's Master Gardener or Natural Resource Steward programs. They represented this year’s gardening strike force, a kind of green-thumbed cavalry that appears at the start of the growing season to ensure that the grounds are in precise harmony with the home they surround. Jan Litvin, Master Gardener, cleans out a birdbath in the perennial garden on the grounds of the Zimmerman House, one of the Frank Lloyd Wright-designed homes owned by the Currier Museum in Manchester. Each year, dozens of expert gardeners, all trained by UNH Extension, help bring the gardens on the property back to a standard of which they think the famed architect would approve. Among the most accomplished of American architects, Frank Lloyd Wright was famously exacting in his design approach, including dimensions and placement of furniture within the homes he created. That level of specificity extended beyond the building itself to the landscaping surrounding it. Such was the case for the Zimmerman House, built in Manchester in 1949, and bequested to the Currier Museum in 1988. By that point, there had been years of deferred maintenance to both the home and landscape, and the first several years of the museum’s ownership were focused on the structure. In 1999, UNH Cooperative Extension was invited to restore the gardens, beginning a long-running partnership that continues to this day. The UNH volunteers get so much heavy lifting done that the gardens can be kept up the rest of the year by a single volunteer, Jane Beaulieu, who has been tending to the Zimmerman House’s flower beds for 20 years. Beaulieu says that her work is directed by a garden plan taken from Wright’s original designs, which made no clear distinction between the structure of the home and the landscape surrounding it. “I have the original plan and we follow it, because this is a museum property and we consider the landscape part of the museum,” Beaulieau says. She has an unusual connection to the property because her mother was treated by Dr. Isadore Zimmerman, who resided there along with his wife Lucille, when Beaulieu was young. Since taking over the gardens, Beaulieau has developed a deeper connection to the property, gained from countless quiet mornings, making sure the gardens are museum-perfect before that day’s tours arrive. She has developed an appreciation for the nuances of the space and its planting, such as in the use of rhododendrons. Along the edge of the property, the perennial flowering bushes are allowed to grow to their full height. In the garden, though, the rhododendron bushes are pruned to about chest-height, which evokes the long, low roofline of the home when viewed from outside and affords an unobstructed view of the backyard from inside. Rhododendron height is just one of the details that Beaulieau aims to get just right. Staying true to Wright’s vision throughout the year is made easier thanks to the cadre of volunteers — all elite gardeners — who contribute a day of labor to the cause. “They work so hard, they don’t stop,” Beaulieau says of the volunteers, estimating that their labor is worth “thousands of dollars” if it were even possible to hire such a crew. “I maintain it after they leave, and it’s so much easier for me because all the hard work is done.” Litvin, one of those volunteers, has been attending the Zimmerman House clean-ups for 20 years, off and on. On this particular clean-up, she’s spending her day edging and weeding a perennial garden and transplanting some ferns, once she scrubs the moss from the bird bath. Litvin keeps coming back because she sees the property as a public amenity, a house in a neighborhood that stands as a reminder that things can be done differently, that modest homes can still be created with great attention to detail. The famed architect would likely have held Litvin’s ilk in high esteem, according to Justin Kedl, who manages the Zimmerman House for the Currier Museum. “Wright’s philosophy was called organic architecture,” Kedl says. “He believed in this close relationship between the house and the landscape itself. He said, ‘Every house is an indoor garden, and every garden is an outdoor house.’” When designing a home, Wright considered the contours of the land, the kinds of wood and stone that would naturally exist there, and the way that sun and shade developed throughout the day. “This day is really, really important to us, to get the landscape back to where it was supposed to be, and then keep it that way going forward,” Kedl says. Now nearly 80 years old, the Zimmerman House continues to speak to visitors today, Kedl says, as an example of “a very intentional way of designing, and an intentional way of living. Most houses don’t look like this today. Visitors see all these small choices that can add up to a more beautiful and intentional life.” As she banishes the last of the moss from the birdbath, Litvin concurs. “It’s like an art treasure that’s hidden away,” says Litvin, “It’s a different way of looking at things, even how to place a home on a lot or what to focus on within a home to make it a sanctuary or a work of art, really.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. This sell-off for America’s largest medical insurer came despite its solid headline numbers, as short-term traders earned profits following the stock's strong run-up into the release. For long-term investors, such temporary dips in high-quality industry leaders often open up compelling entry points, particularly when backed by solid operational fundamentals. The company’s raised profit outlook for the full year may further encourage them to do so. However, membership losses due to rising healthcare costs and continued margin pressure at its Medicaid business, thanks to major funding cuts by the U.S. government in Medicaid funding, remain some major headwinds for this stock. Although its membership retention was better than previously anticipated, UNH expects its 2026 Medicare Advantage enrollment to decline approximately 1.1 million. title: UnitedHealth Group Incorporated (UNH) and Intuitive Surgical, Inc. (ISRG) Just Showed Why Beating Estimates Isn’t Enough - Yahoo Finance Australia
content: Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results Two big healthcare companies, UnitedHealth Group Incorporated (NYSE:UNH) and Intuitive Surgical, Inc. (NASDAQ:ISRG) reported earnings the same week in July. Both beat what Wall Street expected. One stock jumped as much as 8%. The other fell as much as 13%. The difference between them shows what actually moves a healthcare stock right now. UnitedHealth Group Incorporated (NYSE:UNH) blew past expectations. Adjusted earnings hit $6.38 a share versus the $4.90 expected, and revenue rose to $112 billion, also beating estimates. The company raised its full-year profit forecast to $19.50-$20 a share, up from "more than $18.25," a bigger raise than Wall Street hoped for. The stock climbed as much as 8% on the news. The main number was the medical cost ratio, which measures how much of collected premiums gets spent on care. It came in at 86.7%, better than the roughly 88.5% expected and improved from 89.4% a year ago. CFO Wayne DeVeydt said the gain came from plan-design changes, higher premiums, and tighter cost management, not from healthcare costs actually falling: "These results are not a reflection of trend bending or coming under control, but rather our efforts to start pushing down what is already an elevated number." UnitedHealth is also spending about $1.5 billion this year on AI to speed up approvals and catch billing errors and recently partnered with Anthropic, per the Wall Street Journal. Its Optum health unit swung from a 15% income decline last quarter to 29% growth this quarter. Not everything was positive. UnitedHealth lost 525,000 members from the previous quarter and expects to lose roughly 1.6 million more by year-end, mostly as rising costs push people out of coverage. DeVeydt called that trend "not a good thing for the system long term," even as higher prices on remaining customers offset the lost revenue for now. Intuitive Surgical, Inc. (NASDAQ:ISRG), maker of the da Vinci surgical robot, also beat estimates. Revenue rose 19% to $2.89 billion, above the $2.82 billion expected, and adjusted profit hit $2.80 a share versus $2.50 expected. None of it mattered. The stock had climbed as much as 4.2% earlier in the day, then fell as much as 13% after the earnings call and stayed there into the next session, touching its lowest price in over two years. As of July 23, it's down over 40% for the year against an 8% gain for the S&P 500. The issue was guidance, not the quarter itself. Intuitive kept its full-year forecast range unchanged at 13.5%-15.5% procedure growth but said it now expects to land near the middle of that range rather than higher in it as previously implied, a real softening even though the range itself didn't move. Worldwide procedure growth was nearly 15% for the quarter, down from 16% in Q1. In the U.S. specifically, it slowed more sharply, to 12% from 14%, the slowest U.S. pace in three years. CEO David Rosa said insurance and subsidy changes are pushing some patients to delay treatment, and GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are cutting into bariatric surgery volume, which fell by high single digits. Not everyone buys the concern. Abbott had dismissed the same ACA-subsidy worry as a "flawed assumption" the day before and raised its own forecast. Evercore's Vijay Kumar said the softness "rekindles the debate," while Leerink's Mike Kratky called the selloff "increasingly overblown." At least a dozen brokerages cut price targets anyway. Adding pressure, Johnson & Johnson just won approval for its own soft-tissue surgical robot, a new competitor in a market Intuitive has dominated for two decades. If both companies beat estimates, why did one stock soar and the other plummet? Because beating last quarter matters less than what a company says comes next. UnitedHealth Group Incorporated (NYSE:UNH) raised its forecast by a wide margin, signaling its cost improvements are durable. Intuitive Surgical, Inc. (NASDAQ:ISRG) beat too but pointed to a weaker spot inside an unchanged range and confirmed that two real headwinds, i.e., insurance-driven delays in care and GLP-1 drugs cutting into bariatric surgery, were already showing up in its Q2 numbers and not just future risks. Investors reward confidence about the future far more than a solid quarter that's already over. Insider Monkey's hedge fund database shows both stocks losing support before either report came out. UnitedHealth Group Incorporated (NYSE:UNH) was held by 130 funds at the end of Q1 2026, down from 145, with dollar value held falling from $14.8 billion to $9.9 billion. Intuitive Surgical, Inc. (NASDAQ:ISRG) saw a similar pullback, 103 funds versus 109, with value held dropping from $9.2 billion to $8.2 billion. Both stocks were already losing hedge fund conviction before this earnings news, a sign the broader healthcare sector has been out of favor, not just these two names. Same industry, same week, opposite reactions, and the lesson repeats across earnings season: a beat only matters with a reason to believe it continues. UnitedHealth Group Incorporated (NYSE:UNH) earned that belief with a guidance raise backed by real cost improvements. Intuitive Surgical, Inc. (NASDAQ:ISRG) lost investors by confirming two genuine headwinds, insurance changes and GLP-1 drugs, are already hitting its numbers before J&J's new competition even enters the picture. The University of New Hampshire has appointed Ryan Colton as its next director of athletics. Colton, who currently serves as deputy athletics director and chief of staff at the University of Richmond, will lead UNH's 20-sport NCAA Division I athletics program and join the university's senior leadership team. In a press release, UNH said Colton brings 15 years of senior leadership experience in Division I athletics and higher education. He spent eight years with the University of Richmond, whose football teams competed against UNH as Coastal Athletic Association rivals. "Ryan has the vision, experience and judgment to lead UNH Athletics at a pivotal moment in college sports," said UNH President Elizabeth S. Chilton. "He understands the rapidly changing Division I landscape and what it will take to position our programs for sustained competitive success." UNH said Colton helped lead Richmond through a period of significant growth and change while serving as the athletics director's chief adviser on strategic and operational matters. "The University of New Hampshire represents everything I value about higher education and intercollegiate athletics: a commitment to student success, access to opportunity and the pursuit of excellence," Colton said. Before joining Richmond, Colton served as assistant athletics director at the College of the Holy Cross. Previously, he served as special assistant to the director of athletics at Providence College, where he worked on strategic projects and initiatives on behalf of the department. In addition to his athletics leadership experience, Colton has held several public service and legal positions, including serving as a city councilor and council president in Taunton, Mass., practicing law in private practice and serving as a staff member in the Massachusetts Senate. Colton succeeds Allison Rich, who led UNH Athletics from 2022-2026. His start date hasn't been announced. Comments Off on UNH Poll Finds Affordability Pressures Pushing Significant Share of Massachusetts Residents Toward Moving Out BOSTON — High housing prices and the rising cost of living are pushing a significant portion of Massachusetts residents to consider leaving the Bay State, according to fresh polling released this month by the University of New Hampshire Survey Center. View or download the full survey HERE. The survey, conducted online between June 18 and 23 among 709 Massachusetts adults, found that 29% of residents say they definitely or probably want to move out of the commonwealth. An even larger share — 34% — indicated they are likely to relocate within the next five years. The poll carries a margin of error of 3.7%. Among those likely to leave, 70% pointed to cheaper housing or a lower overall cost of living as an important factor. More than half cited a desire for lower taxes, while 39% mentioned seeking a different political or social environment. Stark contrast on livability vs. affordabilityThe findings paint a nuanced picture. While 68% of residents described Massachusetts as a “good” or “very good” place to live — a rating higher than those given by residents of Vermont, Rhode Island, or Connecticut in companion surveys — perceptions of affordability remain dismal. Only 15% called the state an affordable place to live, with 85% saying it is not. This aligns with a separate UNH poll released in late June, in which a majority of residents identified housing or the cost of living as the most pressing issue facing Massachusetts. Where people say they would goThese sentiments come amid documented population losses. U.S. Census Bureau data show Massachusetts experienced a net loss of 33,340 residents between 2024 and 2025, following a net outflow of about 19,000 the previous year. The UNH findings are part of a larger set of simultaneous polls examining quality-of-life perceptions across New England. Comparable surveys released the same week found even higher shares of residents in Connecticut (40%), Vermont (42%), and Rhode Island (35%) saying they are likely to move out in the next five years. New Hampshire recorded the lowest figure in the region at 23%. No quick fixes in sightExperts and local leaders have long pointed to Massachusetts’ acute housing shortage, restrictive zoning, high property taxes in some areas, and elevated overall living expenses as persistent challenges. The new poll data suggest these issues are translating into concrete thoughts of relocation for roughly one-third of the population. At the same time, the strong majority who still rate the state positively indicate that Massachusetts retains significant draws — from job opportunities and education to cultural amenities and natural beauty — for most residents. The full UNH Survey Center report, titled “Most Bay Staters Believe Massachusetts is a Good But Unaffordable Place to Live,” was released on July 7, 2026, and is available through the University of New Hampshire Scholars’ Repository. As policymakers grapple with housing production goals and tax policy debates heading into the fall, the poll serves as a clear signal: for a growing number of Bay Staters, the question is no longer just whether they can afford to stay — but whether they want to. UnitedHealth Group Incorporated is an American multinational for-profit organization that specializes in health insurance and healthcare services, located in Eden Prairie, Minnesota. Operating under the UnitedHealthcare brand for insurance products and the Optum brand for healthcare services, it is recognized as the world's seventh-largest company by revenue and the largest healthcare corporation by revenue. title: UNH Stock Under Pressure Ahead Of Q1 Print: Can Optum Recovery Offset Medicare Advantage Headwinds? - Stocktwits
content: UnitedHealth Group (UNH) heads into its quarterly earnings report due Tuesday, with investors watching whether recovery at Optum, its healthcare services and care-delivery arm, can begin to offset Medicare payment pressure that erased billions from expected revenue. UNH stock slipped 0.4% on Monday to end at $323.48, but rose 0.5% in extended trading. Piper Sandler reiterated an 'Overweight' rating and a $399 price target, implying a 23% upside from current levels ahead of Tuesday’s first-quarter (Q1) results. The brokerage adjusted its expectations for when Optum Health is likely to generate most of its profits this year, but said its updated forecast still aligns with the company’s guidance that nearly two-thirds of 2026 earnings per share should come in the first half of the year. Piper Sandler expects UNH to post adjusted earnings of about $17.79 per share in 2026, broadly in line with the company’s guidance and close to Wall Street’s estimate of $17.89. This would mark an increase from $16.35 per share in 2025, even as revenue is expected to exceed $439 billion. The brokerage firm added it would “continue to be buyers of multi-year turnarounds at UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health.” Separately, Jefferies raised its price target on UnitedHealth shares to $373 from $340 while maintaining a 'Buy' rating, representing a 15% upside from current levels following adjustments to estimates across its managed-care coverage universe. Despite bullish analyst updates, Medicare Advantage reimbursement changes remain the primary driver of UnitedHealth’s earnings recovery. Risk-adjustment revisions introduced over the past several years have already removed billions of dollars from expected revenue and are estimated to have a $6 billion remaining impact into 2026, Bloomberg noted. The company’s exposure is especially significant as UnitedHealth serves over 8 million Medicare Advantage members, the largest footprint in the industry, making payment revisions noteworthy for its earnings outlook. Much of the bull case for UNH stock now depends on the performance of Optum Health, historically one of the company’s biggest drivers of profit growth before changes to Medicare Advantage risk-adjustment payment formulas last year reduced expected reimbursements and pushed the unit into a loss. The company responded by scaling back higher-risk care arrangements and exiting Medicare Advantage plans in 109 counties, affecting 180,000 members. In January, the insurer said during its earnings call that the unit entered 2026 on a “stronger foundation” after reducing its exposure to underperforming risk-based contracts. Investor sentiment toward UNH shares came under fresh pressure earlier this year after regulators initially proposed a near-flat 0.09% Medicare Advantage payment increase for 2027, triggering a sector-wide selloff that erased $60 billion in market value in a single session. Final reimbursement updates later improved to 2.48%, helping stabilize sentiment across insurers. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for UNH jumped to ‘bullish’ from ‘neutral’ levels a day ago amid over a 1,150% surge in 24-hour message volumes. One user said, “The fact that today was not green is actually overall positive for tomorrow to have a nice pop up again on guidance. Guidance will be far more important than numbers tomorrow. I’m thinking $400+ by August “ Another user said, “ER shouldn’t stress longs. Just another dividend payment processed. UNH will be back stronger then ever before. Maybe not tomorrow, but longs will have the last laugh here.” For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com.
